newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy promises full probe into Somalia horrors.
newsitem.headline: Italy promises full probe into Somalia horrors.

text.p: Italy said on Friday it would launch a full inquiry into allegations that troops on a peacekeeping mission to Somalia tortured and sexually abused Somalis and killed unarmed civilians.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi expressed deep concern about the alleged brutality, reported in the news magazine Panorama, and said the cabinet had approved a joint civilian and military commission to investigate the affair.

He promised swift action to identify culprits as outraged reaction to the Panorama report, illustrated by photographs of purported sexual violence against a Somali woman, poured in from political parties and the Vatican.
"These episodes must be checked and we must analyse where the responsibilities lie," Prodi told a news conference.
"We must be very severe in our intervention in order to stop these sorts of episodes happening again," he said.

The commission, initiated by the Defence Ministry, will include both sexes and aims "to ascertain the scale and extent of deviant behaviour inside the armed forces during the operation in Somalia", a cabinet statement said.

The Panorama reports, launched last week with allegations by a former soldier of torture of Somalis, have shocked Italians and embarrassed the military. Italy sent troops to Somalia in late 1992 as part of a U.S-led humanitarian mission.

President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro on Friday called a meeting for next Wednesday of Italy's Supreme Defence Council, a body which convenes only rarely, to hear a report from defence chief Admiral Guido Venturoni on "international missions by the Italian armed forces".
Panorama carried fresh reports of alleged abuses in its latest edition on Friday, backed by photographs and interviews with two more former soldiers.

One series of photographs showed what Panorama said was the sadistic sexual assault of a young Somali woman at an Italian checkpoint, codenamed "Demon", on the road from Mogadishu to Balad in late November 1993.

The photographs, taken by an ex-member of the elite Folgore paratroop division, appeared to show the woman tied by her ankles to an armoured car, in a state of undress and being violated with a military flare.

"She was screaming and struggling, not so much because of the physical pain, perhaps, but because she didn't want it to happen," the former soldier who took the photographs, named only as Stefano, told Panorama.

Another ex-soldier, former fusilier Benedetto Bertini, told Panorama that he believed Italian troops had killed at least six unarmed Somali civilians in a jeep near Belet Huen on the Somali border with Ethiopia.
"We were in a column. We received a radio message saying: 'Don't worry if you hear shots. We're target-shooting Somalis'," he was quoted as saying.
He said that when his patrol reached the scene, the jeep had been destroyed with rifle grenades and its occupants lay dead.
"We were told (by our instructors) that we shouldn't treat Somalis like human beings...The order was: 'If in doubt, fire' even if they were women and children," Bertini said.
The reports of abuse have broken as Italy seeks to raise its international profile through leadership of a multinational security force deployed in Albania since April.
Prodi said the Somalia scandal would not undermine the reputation of Italy's troops in Albania.
"This episode...has nothing to do with our mission and the dedication that our troops have always showed in peace-keeping and are showing now in Albania," he said.
